title: Μύες καὶ γαλαῖ
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 237. Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.l: For mice and weasels there was war.
sentences.i: There was war between the mice and the weasels.
sentences.n: The dative names the parties who had the war on their hands — the same construction as the dative of possession.

sentences.t: Ἀεὶ δὲ οἱ μύες ἡττώμενοι, ἐπειδὴ συνῆλθον εἰς ταὐτόν, ὑπέλαβον ὅτι δι’ ἀναρχίαν τοῦτο πάσχουσιν· ὅθεν ἐπιλεξάμενοί τινας ἑαυτῶν στρατηγοὺς ἐχειροτόνησαν.
sentences.tr: Aei de hoi myes hēttōmenoi, epeidē synēlthon eis tauton, hypelabon hoti di’ anarchian touto paschousin· hothen epilexamenoi tinas heautōn stratēgous echeirotonēsan.
sentences.l: And the mice, being always beaten, when they came together into the same place, supposed that they suffer this through want of a leader; and so, having picked out certain of their own number, they elected them generals.
sentences.i: The mice, always getting the worst of it, came together in one place and concluded that it was for want of a leader that they fared so; and so they picked out some of their own number and elected them generals.
sentences.n: ταὐτόν is τὸ αὐτό run together by crasis, 'the same place'. After ὅτι the mice's own present tense πάσχουσιν is kept. χειροτονέω is the Athenian word for electing by a show of hands, and ἀναρχία for the absence of a magistrate: the mice hold a perfectly regular assembly.

sentences.t: Οἱ δὲ βουλόμενοι ἐπισημότεροι τῶν ἄλλων φανῆναι, κέρατα κατασκευάσαντες ἑαυτοῖς συνῆψαν.
sentences.tr: Hoi de boulomenoi episēmoteroi tōn allōn phanēnai, kerata kataskeuasantes heautois synēpsan.
sentences.l: And they, wishing to appear more conspicuous than the rest, having made horns, fastened them onto themselves.
sentences.i: And the generals, wanting to look more distinguished than the rest, made horns and fastened them on themselves.
sentences.n: ἐπίσημος is 'marked, bearing a device' — what is on the coin or the shield — so the horns are an insignia of office rather than a weapon. Nothing in the Greek says the horns were any use in a fight.

sentences.t: Ἐνστάσης δὲ τῆς μάχης, συνέβη πάντας τοὺς μύας ἡττηθῆναι.
sentences.tr: Enstasēs de tēs machēs, synebē pantas tous myas hēttēthēnai.
sentences.l: And the battle having set in, it came about that all the mice were defeated.
sentences.i: When battle was joined, it turned out that all the mice were beaten.
sentences.n: ἐνίστημι of a war or a season is 'to be upon us, set in'. συμβαίνει takes an accusative and infinitive for the thing that came to pass.

sentences.t: Οἱ μὲν οὖν ἄλλοι πάντες ἐπὶ τὰς ὀπὰς καταφεύγοντες ῥᾳδίως εἰσέδυνον· οἱ δὲ στρατηγοὶ μὴ δυνάμενοι εἰσελθεῖν διὰ τὰ κέρατα αὐτῶν συλλαμβανόμενοι κατησθίοντο.
sentences.tr: Hoi men oun alloi pantes epi tas opas katapheugontes rhāidiōs eisedynon· hoi de stratēgoi mē dynamenoi eiselthein dia ta kerata autōn syllambanomenoi katēsthionto.
sentences.l: Now all the rest, fleeing for refuge to their holes, slipped in easily; but the generals, not being able to get in because of their horns, being caught, were eaten up.
sentences.i: So all the rest ran for their holes and slipped in easily; but the generals could not get in because of their horns, and were caught and eaten.
sentences.n: εἰσδύνω is to slip in, the exact verb for a mouse and a hole. The imperfect κατησθίοντο draws the end out: they were being eaten one after another.

sentences.t: Οὕτω πολλοῖς ἡ κενοδοξία κακῶν αἰτία γίνεται.
sentences.tr: Houtō pollois hē kenodoxia kakōn aitia ginetai.
sentences.l: So for many vainglory becomes a cause of evils.
sentences.n: κενοδοξία is literally 'empty opinion' — the appetite for being thought somebody — and the horns are the fable's picture of it.
